vignette:
Aisha was 25, a South Asian cybersecurity analyst living with her partner in an apartment near downtown Chicago, and the event she kept returning to was a mugging that happened on a winter evening when she had stayed late at work. She had been walking from the train to her building with her laptop bag tucked under her arm when two men closed in near the lobby entrance, one shoving her into a narrow service corridor while the other reached for her phone and wallet. The corridor felt brutally tight, the door behind her had latched, and she remembered the harsh smell of concrete and old trash, the sound of her own breathing, and the strange blankness in her body as if her legs had stopped belonging to her. Since then, certain crowded places had become unbearable to move through, and she noticed herself scanning every hallway, elevator, and storefront window for reflections; at work she caught herself checking mirrors in the glass walls of conference rooms and in the shiny black screen of her monitor, as though she needed constant proof of where people were and whether she could still get out.

What had happened stayed with her in a way that did not feel like a memory at all. When she tried to describe it, the words would not come together; she would start, stop, and say it felt easier to keep it as "that night" rather than tell the story from beginning to end. Each time the scene broke through anyway, she caught herself thinking there must be something permanently wrong with her, and that she had been exposed as weak in a way other people would never understand. Each time she brushed past a reminder on the street or at work, the thought arrived with it that she would never stop being afraid, and that the world had become the kind of place where she had to read danger into every ordinary corner. Yet the details forced their way into her mind when she least wanted them to, often in the middle of routine moments-someone mentioning a train platform, a coworker joking about being cornered by deadlines, a friend talking about safety alarms-and suddenly she was back in the corridor, feeling the pressure of the wall against her shoulder and the panic in her throat. In those moments the event seemed to be happening right now, not in the past, and she would freeze, flush hot with humiliation, and tell herself that the world no longer worked the way she had assumed it did. On nights when she felt most exposed, that same sense of danger kept her close to the attack in her mind, as if she had to keep replaying it to stay one step ahead of what might come next. The memory would surface with particular force then, vivid and unwelcome. She had come to believe that what happened had destroyed any ordinary faith in safety, and more personally, that her own body had betrayed her by going weak and silent when she needed it to hold firm. That sense of being permanently humiliated sat close to every attempt to explain it, and the more she tried to put the memory out of reach-by erasing details, pushing away anything that might stir either sadness or relief, and refusing to dwell on what she felt-the more brittle and unfinished the memory remained.

Her fears then spread outward into daily life. Crowded sidewalks near her office, packed elevators in her building, and crowded places after dark all became places to avoid or rush through, because the crush of bodies seemed to echo that corridor and she felt exposed the second she could not see enough exits. If the world was dangerous and she was not ready for it, then staying on the edge of rooms, checking mirrors, and choosing the emptiest route home felt to her like the only sensible way to get through the day. Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she could not stop reading; almost anything-a man standing too close in the lobby, a van idling by the curb, voices raised near the train platform-could tip into a warning and bring the old fear rushing back. The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made those ordinary details feel charged, as if they were confirming what her body had already decided was true. Conversation topics that touched on street crime, break-ins, or anyone's close call were especially hard for her to tolerate, not only because they could pull the memory back into her mind but because they also made her feel foolish for ever thinking she had been safe. The same was true at home when she and her partner talked about moving neighborhoods or about late-night errands; she would become tense, irritable, and abruptly change the subject, then later replay the exchange and feel ashamed of how sharp she had sounded. She had been trying for so long not to talk about it, not to picture it, and not to let herself feel too much that when the memory did break through, it came back sharper than she expected, as if all that pushing away had kept it intact and close. By keeping it at a distance, she had never really placed it anywhere in the past, so when it surfaced it returned with a force that made it feel freshly dangerous all over again. She noticed that the more she avoided feeling anything at all, the narrower her life became, yet she kept doing it because she feared that any strong feeling-panic, anger, even tenderness-might crack open the night she had been attacked.

At night the world felt especially unsafe. Aisha found herself listening for footsteps in the hallway, double-checking the lock on the apartment door, and waking to peer out through the blinds or glance at the dark shapes reflected in mirrors and windows. She became more irritable at work and at home, snapping in meetings, taking too many risks on the road to prove to herself she was not afraid, and then feeling embarrassed by how reckless she had become. The more vigilant she felt at night, the more likely the memory was to intrude; the more the memory intruded, the more she concluded that she still could not trust her body or the world, and the more she avoided crowded routes, enclosed spaces, and certain conversations that might stir it. Her partner noticed that she had grown distant and jumpy, and Aisha herself was alarmed by how much the days were being organized around what might trigger the next surge of fear.

She came for help when she realized she was starting to shape her work and social life around escape routes, mirror checks, and silence, and when that pattern began to make her feel as though the mugging was still running her life. What she wanted most was to stop feeling trapped by the corridor in her mind, and what she feared most was that if she let herself really remember, she would be overwhelmed all over again.
